skip_reason: Post-move service-recovery and damage-claim call, not a sales conversation. Rance opened it himself as a callback on an existing complaint — 'I got a message from one of my customer service [team] about your move today. So, I was just calling to follow up with you and see what we can do for you' — and the entire thirteen minutes is a completed-move escalation: a damaged $3,500 table, patio furniture left behind at the origin requiring a second trip, a billing refund for the wasted time, and whether an on-site damage claim was successfully filed. No quote, no estimate, no booking, no pricing structure, and no prospect. There is nothing on the 85-point Sales Call Scorecard that applies. Note for routing: this is a claims escalation, which sits in Amanda's interim coverage rather than in the sales grading population.
top_strength: Not graded against the sales rubric, but worth recording because the service-recovery handling here is strong enough to be a training example. Rance set expectations honestly in the first thirty seconds rather than overpromising: 'my branch manager is out today. I'm one of the management team, the guy who can actually handle like refunds and stuff with you. We'll be back in tomorrow, so, I kinda just wanted to go over some of your concerns and take some notes on it. So I can pass along to him and have him prepared.' He then let a furious repeat customer talk without interrupting through a long, detailed complaint, and when he responded he committed to something concrete and verifiable on the first issue: 'we'll be able to refund the time for the crew that was gone on that job to go back, our trucks all have trackers in there, so we can track the time that it took to leave and come back for you.' When the customer immediately widened the ask — 'It's that time plus the time lost of having four able body gentlemen moving at the new place' — Rance did not haggle: 'Yeah, yeah. Yeah we'll take that in the consideration we'll offer you, yeah, you know we wanna make things right.' On the damaged table he named the company standard the crew violated, which is the single most credibility-restoring thing a manager can do: 'that's quite frankly not up to our standards. One of the things that we evaluate guys on and as part of our practices is that we are supposed to disassemble things like that before we take it out of a unit... I know it doesn't fix what happened for you on the job but I do want to let you know that isn't within our policy.' He caught the real root issue unprompted — that the crew knew about the damage and said nothing until the customer found it — and addressed it directly: 'we want our movers to take accountability and if they do damage stuff, you know, mistakes do happen... when something does happen, we want our movers to point it out to the customer on site.' He was careful not to overpromise on the $2,000 coverage, framing it accurately rather than reassuringly ('That is a case by case basis depending on you know, what the damages are... So that's not a hard solid thing'), told the customer he still has a couple of weeks to add items to the claim, and closed with an explicit reason for calling on a Sunday evening: 'I know disappointed in the service so I just didn't want to, you know, sit overnight and wait till tomorrow and making, not feel like you were heard.' The customer went from 'this is the worst moving experience I've had in 25 or thirty years' and 'I'm questioning if I ever use your company again' to 'Well, I appreciate you making the time' and 'Okay, thank you. I appreciate it.' That is a retained customer.
coaching_note: Not graded — skipped as a non-sales call. Three things worth surfacing to Amanda anyway, since claims sit in her interim coverage until Carly is back and two of these are operational rather than individual. First, the damage claim may not exist. The customer's account is that the on-site filing failed: 'he started to try to fill it out and I guess you have to take pictures and the pictures weren't loading properly. So it kept kicking them out of the system and then he was like, well let me just load one... So I believe he uploaded it. But I can't tell you with certainty that he did.' A photo-upload failure that kicks a foreman out of the claim form mid-filing is a tooling problem, not a crew problem, and if it is reproducible it is silently dropping claims across every branch. Worth checking whether this is a known failure mode before it is written off as one crew's carelessness. Rance committed to confirming receipt the next morning and to sending a filing link if it never landed, which is the right follow-through. Second, the coaching items Rance identified are correct and specific, and they map directly to existing training: disassemble two-piece tables before taking them through a doorway rather than forcing them ('they tried to manually pull it out of the door and like shove it through the door and it scraped the entire table'), do a final sweep so nothing is left behind (patio furniture was missed at the origin, and the customer had already flagged it verbally to the lead — 'I said, hey, don't forget the patio furniture. He's like, okay, I got it'), and self-report damage to the customer on site instead of waiting to be caught. The second one cost Einstein real money on this job: a return trip, a second freight elevator cycle, and four movers idle at the destination, all of which is now being refunded. Third, this is a repeat customer whose first Einstein move was excellent — 'my first experience with y'all was great which is why I did it again. That first crew, no problem' — which makes the delta a crew-level execution issue rather than a brand one, and makes the recovery worth doing properly. He also did not tip, which he flagged as unprecedented for him, and explicitly did not want anyone fired. One process note for Rance himself: he committed Daniel to a callback the next morning twice, and the customer has now been promised a call about the refund and a call about the claim status. Those need to be one call, or the customer experiences a second round of being handed around.
phone_presence_notes: Let a furious repeat customer finish a long complaint without interrupting, validated before defending ('Yes sir, I am. Yes, sir. Yeah, no, I understand'), named his own company's failure in plain terms rather than hedging ('it's just unacceptable, it's against our company standards'), and volunteered why he was calling on a Sunday evening at all ('I just didn't want to sit overnight and wait till tomorrow and make you not feel like you were heard') — taking the customer from 'the worst moving experience I've had in 25 or thirty years' to 'I appreciate you making the time' inside thirteen minutes.
